blocks.text: Treating viral infections is fundamentally different from treating bacterial ones. Bacteria are independent living organisms, while viruses are parasites that are not truly alive on their own: they live inside our cells and use our own DNA/RNA machinery to replicate. This makes it hard to develop a drug that kills the virus without harming our healthy cells.

blocks.title: Mutation
blocks.text: Viruses can change their genetic material very quickly; this is called mutation. A drug that works against a virus one year might not work the next, because the virus has changed. This is why flu vaccines need to be updated every year.

Some viruses also integrate into our genome or stay inactive ('asleep') in our cells for years, and present drugs can kill only active viruses. Antiviral medicines work by targeting specific stages of the viral life cycle: some prevent the virus from entering our cells, while others stop the virus copying its genetic material. One of the most common mechanisms is enzyme inhibition. Protease inhibitors, for example, are used in treating HIV and hepatitis C infections. Some antiviral drugs strengthen the immune response instead; interferons are proteins that boost the immune system to fight viruses.

blocks.title: What protease inhibitors block
blocks.text: The book says a protease inhibitor 'does not allow the virus to produce their protein in one long strand'. In fact the virus makes its proteins as one long strand, and its protease enzyme cuts this strand into working proteins; protease inhibitors block that cutting, so new viruses cannot mature.

blocks.alt: Four boxes for the stages of viral replication: the virus enters the cell; its genetic material is copied; viral proteins are made as one long strand and cut to size; new viruses leave the cell. Red crosses link the first three stages to red boxes: some antivirals stop the virus entering, others stop copies of the genetic material, and protease inhibitors stop the strand being cut. A line notes that interferons boost the immune system. A panel lists why they are hard to treat.
blocks.caption: Where antiviral drugs act (original diagram for topic 32.4).
blocks.long_description: Each antiviral drug blocks one stage of the virus's life cycle. Because the virus uses the host cell's own machinery, a drug that blocks a stage can also affect the cell.

blocks.prompt: Drug A has a TI of 3 and drug B a TI of 50. Which drug is safer, and why?
blocks.explanation: Drug B: its toxic dose is 50 times its effective dose, a much larger safety margin than drug A's.

blocks.prompt: How do antacids such as magnesium hydroxide regulate stomach pH? Write a neutralisation equation.
blocks.explanation: The base neutralises excess stomach acid, raising the pH: Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O.

blocks.prompt: Identify the strained ring system in penicillin that is essential for its antibacterial activity.
blocks.explanation: The four-membered beta-lactam ring (fused to the thiazolidine ring).

blocks.prompt: Compare the structures of morphine and codeine (methylmorphine). How does this small difference relate to codeine acting as a prodrug?
blocks.explanation: Codeine is morphine with one OH group (the phenolic OH) changed to OCH3. This makes codeine bind weakly to opioid receptors; in the liver some codeine is demethylated back to morphine, which gives most of the pain relief, so codeine acts as a prodrug.

blocks.prompt: Why do many antiviral drugs cause significant side effects for the patient?
blocks.explanation: Viruses replicate using the host cell's own machinery, so drugs that block viral replication can also interfere with the patient's healthy cells.

items: Viruses live in our cells and use our machinery; they mutate fast.
Antivirals block entry, copying of genetic material or protein processing (protease inhibitors).
